**Main question:** How does accounting for species and sex change our description of penguin body measurements and the relationships between them?

You will combine boxplots, one-dimensional kernel density estimates (KDEs), stratified scatterplots, Pearson correlations and comparisons within groups. All analyses are descriptive: focus on the direction, strength and shape of the observed patterns. A final optional section introduces bivariate density contours. Work through Sections 1–6 before attempting Section 7.

**Student task — work with your group.**

The observational unit is a penguin in the Palmer Archipelago dataset. The measurements were collected in 2007–2009. The dataset contains three species and both numerical and categorical variables.

Before each analysis, write a prediction. Then add your code and explain whether the result supports it. Keep the supplied setup; replace the TODO comments with your work. The uncompleted template can be knitted, but it will not contain your answers.

## Getting started

Open this file in RStudio and choose **Knit** to produce an HTML report. Install the packages below once, from the console. Place this Rmd in the folder that contains the `data` folder; the supplied dataset must be at `data/penguins.csv`. When running chunks interactively, use that same folder as the working directory. The CSV is a local copy of the Palmer Penguins data distributed by the `palmerpenguins` project; its provenance and citation are given below. You do not need to install that data package. `MASS` is used only for the optional bivariate KDE section.

```{r installation, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "MASS", "knitr", "rmarkdown"))
```

```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = TRUE,
  fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, dpi = 120)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
set.seed(314159)
data_file <- file.path("data", "penguins.csv")
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  stop("Cannot find data/penguins.csv. Put the data folder next to this Rmd file.")
}
p_raw <- read.csv(data_file, stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                  na.strings = c("", "NA"), strip.white = TRUE)
required <- c("species", "island", "sex", "body_mass_g",
              "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")
missing_columns <- setdiff(required, names(p_raw))
if (length(missing_columns)) {
  stop("Missing CSV columns: ", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", "))
}
# CSV files do not preserve R factor levels: recreate them explicitly.
p_raw$species <- trimws(p_raw$species)
p_raw$sex <- tolower(trimws(p_raw$sex))
stopifnot(all(na.omit(p_raw$species) %in% c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo")),
          all(na.omit(p_raw$sex) %in% c("female", "male")))
p_raw$species <- factor(p_raw$species, levels = c("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"))
p_raw$sex <- factor(p_raw$sex, levels = c("female", "male"))
p_raw$island <- factor(trimws(p_raw$island))
numeric_columns <- c("body_mass_g", "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")
stopifnot(all(vapply(p_raw[numeric_columns], is.numeric, logical(1))))
p_raw$row_id <- seq_len(nrow(p_raw))
species_colours <- c(Adelie = "#D55E00", Chinstrap = "#0072B2", Gentoo = "#009E73")

# Analysis populations: each excludes only the variables needed for that task.
p_mass <- p_raw[complete.cases(p_raw[c("body_mass_g", "species", "sex")]), ]
p_bill <- p_raw[complete.cases(p_raw[c("bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "species")]), ]

# We use sample quartiles (R quantile type 7), not boxplot.stats() hinges.
flag_iqr <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75), type = 7, names = FALSE)
  spread <- q[2] - q[1]
  x < q[1] - 1.5 * spread | x > q[2] + 1.5 * spread
}
```

Keep the same analysis rows when comparing graphical summaries. Record any exclusions and their reasons. Use units in axis labels, common scales for comparable panels, and captions stating the population or subgroup shown.

# Looking ahead: from simple to multiple linear regression

**Remark — connecting with what you already know.** You have studied simple linear regression. Here we describe the direction and strength of linear associations using Pearson correlations and scatterplots. Later, multiple linear regression will allow you to consider several variables together and handle continuous covariates without dividing them into many small groups. The comparisons within species and sex provide a graphical introduction to that idea; no multiple regression is needed in this activity.

# Data and references

- Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2022). *Palmer Archipelago Penguins Data in the palmerpenguins R Package — An Alternative to Anderson's Irises*. [The R Journal](https://rjournal.github.io/articles/RJ-2022-020/).
- [Dataset documentation and provenance](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/). Data are available under CC0. Original field data were collected by Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research programme. This activity uses a CSV copy of the curated `penguins` dataset, retaining its original variable names. Providing a CSV changes the access method, not the source of the data; no installation of `palmerpenguins` is needed.
- [Univariate KDE in ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density.html) and [bivariate density contours](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_density_2d.html).
